headline: High risk of prompt injection and cascading errors: kotaemon’s broad file/API ingestion can feed oh-my-openagent’s MCP-driven workflows, creating unsafe default interactions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: kotaemon ingests documents, HTML, MHTML, PDFs, and chat transcripts, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks plus team messaging APIs. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if kotaemon output or retrieved content is passed into openagent workflows. No direct shared channel is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF kotaemon outputs are copied into oh-my-openagent prompts or hooks
IF a shared workspace or message queue is configured between the two agents
mitigations: Disable automatic handoff of retrieved text into agent prompts
Add a provenance tag to all retrieved snippets before reuse
Restrict hooks to allowlisted commands only
Use separate workspaces for the two agents
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization between retrieval and agent execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: kotaemon touches API keys and broad document types, and oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts plus session history with broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials store, sensitive material can flow from A into B and then out over B’s networked tools. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this remains medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same credential files or workspace
IF kotaemon ingests documents containing secrets that oh-my-openagent later reuses
mitigations: Store API keys in separate secret stores
Mount distinct working directories for each agent
Redact secrets before passing files between agents
Review outbound destinations for oh-my-openagent
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent credential isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances and broad network egress; oh-my-openagent also spawns subprocesses and writes to several config/cache paths, while kotaemon writes to ./ktem_app_data. Overlap is not proven on the same directory, but concurrent writes to shared resources are plausible if co-installed, so the conflict risk exists in default-like setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same project or config directory
IF either agent modifies shared files without locking
mitigations: Assign separate data directories per agent
Avoid concurrent runs against the same repo
Back up shared configs before use
Check for lockfile support in both tools
requires-engineering: add cross-process locking around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: kotaemon is a RAG/chat system that can surface citations and retrieved facts, and oh-my-openagent exposes team_send_message, team_task_create, and other action-oriented APIs. If B consumes A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into external messages or tasks. Because B has downstream action authority and no verification step is documented, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent forwards kotaemon answers into team_send_message or team_task_create
IF no human verification step is inserted before action execution
mitigations: Require human approval before outbound actions
Add a verification prompt before task creation
Limit B to read-only mode for A’s outputs
Log source citations alongside every forwarded claim
requires-engineering: implement confidence-based gating before actions

E_compliance.rationale: kotaemon explicitly handles API keys and chat transcripts, while oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts and session history. If the pair is used on regulated or sensitive data, their differing storage and network behaviors can create retention or residency mismatches. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR boundaries, so this is a compliance-gap risk rather than a residency breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through either agent
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Document data classes allowed in each agent
Set matching retention windows
Exclude regulated records from both tools
Review vendor terms for each deployment
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for retention and deletion
